title: The Problem with Chunking
author: Chris Reid
summary: A UK science teacher and researchED speaker challenges the near-universal classroom advice that instructional content should always be broken into the smallest possible 'chunks,' arguing that cognitive load theory itself contains no such blanket rule and that the evidence for it is considerably more conditional than the advice implies. Drawing on curiosity research showing an 'inverted-U' relationship between difficulty and engagement -- too little complexity produces boredom, too much produces overload -- the piece argues teachers should be asking what level of complexity will cognitively engage a specific student rather than reflexively minimizing complexity for everyone. The centerpiece evidence is the expertise-reversal effect: a study comparing football novices and semi-professional players found that chunked, sequential presentation of a play helped novices remember more with less effort, but actually cost semi-pros more mental effort than seeing the whole formation move at once, since experts already possess the schema to parse a complex scene holistically. The piece closes by citing a Craig Barton Research Bites study in which Austrian adults learning Italian verb conjugation performed best under the hardest, most interleaved version of a task and worst under the easiest, arguing that the same scaffolding that helps low-prior-knowledge students can actively limit students who already have the schema to handle complexity directly.
points: The football expertise-reversal study is the essay's strongest evidence: chunked presentation helped novices and cost them less effort, but for semi-professional players the same chunking increased mental effort, because experts already hold the whole-play schema needed to parse it unbroken.

Curiosity research's 'inverted-U' shape reframes the goal away from 'minimize complexity' (the DfE's stated advice) toward finding the Goldilocks Zone just beyond a specific student's current knowledge, since both under- and over-complexity independently damage learning and engagement.

Cognitive load theory's own content does not license the 'chunk everything smaller' rule commonly derived from it -- the theory is actually about managing element interactivity (how pieces of information relate), not about minimizing raw quantity of information per step.

The Barton Research Bites Italian-verb study, where the hardest interleaved-practice condition outperformed the easiest condition on a delayed test, is used as direct evidence against the assumption that lower difficulty is inherently safer or more supportive for learners with adequate prior knowledge.
quotes: It can guide task design, but there is nothing in cognitive load theory that says smaller chunks of information are always better. In fact, there are situations in which the opposite is true. We need to consider 'element interactivity' -- how new pieces of information relate to one another -- too.

Novices who saw the chunked version remembered more, and it cost them less mental effort. For semi-pros, the format didn't affect their recall -- but the chunked version did cost them more mental effort.
These expert players learned more efficiently when they saw the whole structure at once.
The same scaffolds that provide good support to students with low prior knowledge can limit the learning of those with stronger prior knowledge.

Via Craig Barton's excellent Research Bites, I came across a study comparing the effectiveness of simpler tasks to more complex ones: 132 Austrian adults with no Italian were taught to conjugate an Italian verb. The hardest version with interleaved practice came out best and the easiest task performed worst, when students were tested afterwards. It's time to challenge the advice that smaller is always better.
